title: What Does Done Even Mean? Agents and Paperclip's Liveness Model - Dotta, Paperclip

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 92%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on Paperclip's control plane for agentic work—state transitions, first-class blockers, watchdog agents, and harness-agnostic enforcement—which is squarely agent harness architecture. Examples focus on coding agent workflows involving PRs, tests, and documentation, and Paperclip is a developer platform for orchestrating agent work. The content addresses operational management of agent systems at scale, focusing on work completion, verification, and state management in production-like settings. Requires familiarity with agent workflows and CI/CD concepts but remains conceptual rather than deeply technical. A conference presentation from the AI Engineer channel. Claims are backed by a working open-source system with concrete demonstrations across multiple agent harnesses.

summary: Dotta frames the core problem: agents can now generate code and documentation faster than any human can verify, creating a failure mode where agent output overwhelms review capacity. Saying something is 'done' is actually a bundle of claims—an artifact was produced, evidence exists that the task is complete, a rubric defines the standard, an owner is assigned for the next step, and the next action is clear. Different levels of 'done' exist: a producer claiming completion, a reviewer finding no obvious issues, evidence meeting a specified standard, an authorized approver signing off, someone standing behind the decision, and ideally the outcome surviving real-world conditions. Exhaustive human verification fails at high volume, producing verification theater. The fundamental tension is between liveliness (work continuing without blockers) and verification (human review providing correctness assurance but halting work). No approvals yield AI slop; all peer review yields an unmanageable queue. Paperclip's control plane enforces three invariants: productive work continues, only real blockers stop work, and infinite loops are bounded. Mechanisms include clear state transitions, first-class blockers between tasks enforced by the control plane, interactive human approval with audit trails, explicit reviewers and approvers, and watchdog agents operating in a maximizer mode that are harness-agnostic (working with Pi, OpenGL, Hermes, Claude Code, Codex). Dotta's key advice is to stop treating 'done' as a Boolean and treat it as an object with fields: artifact, scope, rubric, evidence, verifier, authority, remaining risk, and next action. A practical checklist for scaling includes defining 'done' precisely per task, separating the verifier from the author (ideally using a different model—for example, Claude writes and Codex verifies), requiring agents to provide evidence through custom browser harnesses and screenshots, and maintaining a clear chain of custody so every agent knows who receives the work next.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening: The Problem with 'Done'
sections.summary: Dotta opens with a scenario: an agent opens a PR, passes tests, updates docs, closes the issue, and says 'done.' But done enough to merge? To deploy? To announce? These are different operational claims that most agent systems flatten into a single green checkmark.

sections.title: Programming Is Solved: The Verification Crisis
sections.summary: Dotta argues programming is solved and agents produce code faster than humans can verify, creating a new failure mode: agents generating more work than humans have time to verify. Simply letting agents check a checkbox is insufficient.

sections.title: 'Done' as a Bundle of Claims
sections.summary: Saying something is done is a bundle of claims: an artifact was produced, evidence exists, a rubric defines the standard, the next-step owner is known, and the next step is clear. Different levels exist—producer claim, reviewer finding no issues, evidence meeting standard, authorized approval, someone standing behind the decision, and surviving real-world conditions.

sections.title: Verification Theater and the Need for a Protocol
sections.summary: Exhaustive human verification fails at high volume. Humans verifying all tasks leads to verification theater. What's needed is a protocol for task progression through a system—keeping tasks moving without getting stuck in invalid states, with a control plane tying execution to contracts and constraints.

sections.title: Liveliness vs. Verification Tension
sections.summary: The core tension: human review provides correctness assurance but halts work, while liveliness means work continues without blockers. No approvals produce AI slop; full peer review creates unmanageable queues. Naively looping over tasks falls apart with dependency trees, blockers, multiple agents, and checkout locks. The bundle of claims must be teased apart.

sections.title: Three Invariants and Paperclip's Mechanisms
sections.summary: A control plane must ensure three invariants: productive work continues, only real blockers stop work, and infinite loops are bounded. Paperclip implements clear state transitions, first-class blockers enforced by the control plane, interactive human approval with audit trails, explicit reviewers and approvers, and harness-agnostic watchdog agents in maximizer mode that enforce goal completion across Pi, OpenGL, Hermes, Claude Code, and Codex.

sections.title: Treat 'Done' as an Object, Not a Boolean
sections.summary: Dotta advises treating 'done' as an object with fields: artifact, scope, rubric/standard, evidence, who verified, who has authority to sign off, remaining risk, and next action. Humans automatically paper over these details, but agents must distinguish between each claim when stating something is done.

sections.title: Checklist for 100x More Work
sections.summary: Practical checklist: define exactly what 'done' means per task; separate the verifier from the author (ideally different models—Claude writes, Codex verifies); require agents to provide evidence via custom browser harnesses, screenshots, and interactive tooling; maintain a clear chain of custody so every agent knows who receives the work next. Serious, accountable work demands detailed 'done' definitions and structure for agents to verify all claims are met.

evidence.excerpt: An agent opens a pull request. It passes the tests. It updates the documentation. It closes the issue and comments, "Looks done to me." But is it actually done?
evidence.supports: The core problem: agents claim 'done' but done is not a single state—it spans merge, deploy, and announce with different operational claims.

evidence.excerpt: Programming is solved, and agents can now produce more code and documentation faster than any human can ever verify. And this actually gives us a new failure mode, is that agents can actually create more work than humans have time to verify.
evidence.supports: Agents produce work faster than humans can verify, creating a new failure mode of unmanageable verification volume.

evidence.excerpt: Saying that something is done is actually a bundle of claims. You're saying that an artifact was produced, that you have evidence that the task is actually complete, and you have a rubric in which you can verify against.
evidence.supports: Done is a bundle of claims including artifact, evidence, rubric, ownership, and next step—not a single checkbox.

evidence.excerpt: if you have humans verifying all the tasks and they have to sign off on it, you eventually what you just get is a form of verification theater.
evidence.supports: Exhaustive human verification at high volume degrades into verification theater.

evidence.excerpt: Liveliness means that the work is continuing with no blockers. And you're always trying to keep these two things in balance. If you have tasks that are completely alive with no approvals, then what you get is this classic AI slop
evidence.supports: The fundamental tension between liveliness and verification: no approvals yield AI slop, full review yields unmanageable queues.

evidence.excerpt: You want to ensure that productive work continues. You want to make sure that only real blockers stop work. And you want to make sure that infinite loops are bounded.
evidence.supports: Three invariants a control plane must enforce for agentic work.

evidence.excerpt: the watchdog within Paperclip is harness agnostic. You can use it with Pi, OpenGL, Hermes, Claude Code, Codex, whatever you're using, you have one consistent interface for ensuring that goal is complete.
evidence.supports: Paperclip's watchdog agents are harness-agnostic, working across multiple agent frameworks with a consistent interface.

evidence.excerpt: stop treating done as a Boolean and treat it more like an object. This isn't specific to Paperclip. It's just advice on how you think about what is done.
evidence.supports: Key advice: treat done as a structured object, not a Boolean, independent of any specific tool.

evidence.excerpt: You definitely want to separate the verifier from the author. Often, this means you're using a different model. So, if you're coding using Claude, have Codex verify.
evidence.supports: Separate verifier from author using different models to avoid self-verification bias.

evidence.excerpt: if you have serious work that you're accountable for, it's very important that you define what done really means in as much detail as possible, and that you have a structure for your agents, so that way they can verify that all of the claims that are involved with something being done are actually met.
evidence.supports: For serious accountable work, done must be defined in detail with a structure enabling agents to verify all completion claims.
